items.stem: A 25-year-old man has had a dry cough for 3 months. He has allergic rhinitis and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He is a non-smoker and takes no antihypertensive drug. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 80/min, RR 18/min, BP 120/80 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 97%, normal breath sounds. CXR shows normal lung parenchyma. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC 70%, FEV1 76% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: GINA 2024; Harrison 21st ed., Cough and Hemoptysis
items.pearl: Chronic cough + normal CXR + borderline obstructive spirometry in a young atopic patient = asthma (cough-variant). Allergic rhinitis and GERD are the classic associated conditions, not alternative diagnoses.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with old pulmonary tuberculosis coughs up 500 mL of fresh blood within 6 hours. PE: T 37.2 C, PR 118/min, RR 30/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 88%; crepitation over the RIGHT upper lung, clear left lung. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
choices: Give oxygen and place the patient in the right lateral decubitus position with preparation for airway intubation
Place the patient in the left lateral decubitus position to drain the bleeding lung
Start intravenous tranexamic acid and observe in the emergency room
Perform urgent bronchial artery embolization before securing the airway
Start empirical anti-tuberculous drugs and arrange an outpatient CT chest
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Hemoptysis; Fishman Pulmonary Diseases 6th ed.
items.pearl: In massive hemoptysis, death is from asphyxiation, not exsanguination. Bleeding side DOWN protects the good lung, then secure the airway, then localise and embolize.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has had dyspnea on exertion for 2 months without chest pain. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 90/min, RR 24/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 96%, jugular venous pressure 6 cm above the sternal angle, loud P2, no murmur, no distant heart sounds, pitting edema of both legs 3+. Which of the following is the MOST likely mechanism of dyspnea in this patient?
choices: Volume overload from end-stage renal disease
Airflow limitation from small airway obstruction
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 1; ESC/ERS 2022 Pulmonary Hypertension Guideline
items.pearl: Loud P2 + elevated JVP + peripheral edema with clear lungs and normal SpO2 = right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension. Distant heart sounds (not loud P2) would point to tamponade.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had dyspnea for 2 months. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 80/min, RR 22/min, BP 120/80 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 98%, normal breath sounds both lungs. Pulmonary function test shows FEV1/FVC 65%. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 17; ATS/ERS 2022 Interpretation of Pulmonary Function Tests
items.pearl: FEV1/FVC below 70% = obstructive pattern; only asthma on this list is obstructive. Obesity, effusion, atelectasis and consolidation all produce a restrictive pattern (low FVC, preserved ratio).

items.stem: A 65-year-old man has had dyspnea for 4 months and expectorates greyish sputum every morning. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 80/min, RR 22/min, BP 140/90 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 97%, increased AP diameter of the chest wall, normal breath sounds both lungs. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 68% and FEV1 75% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 16; GOLD 2024 Report
items.pearl: COPD requires a POST-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 that does not normalise. FEV1 75% predicted places this patient in GOLD grade 2.

items.stem: A 60-year-old farmer has had progressive dyspnea for 1 year. PE: RR 24/min, SpO2 (room air) 92%, fine late-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and clubbing of the fingers. Spirometry: FVC 60% predicted, FEV1 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 82%, DLCO 45% predicted. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: ATS/ERS 2022 PFT interpretation; Harrison 21st ed., Interstitial Lung Disease
items.pearl: Restrictive spirometry WITH a low DLCO means the parenchyma is diseased. Restriction with a NORMAL DLCO points to chest wall, obesity or neuromuscular causes.

items.stem: A 30-year-old asthmatic woman comes to the emergency room with progressive dyspnea and non-productive cough for 3 days. She stopped her inhaled corticosteroid 3 months ago and has used her reliever inhaler daily for the past week, three times in the last hour. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 120/min, RR 30/min, BP 140/90 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 90%, generalized expiratory wheezing. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial treatment?
choices: Oxygen supplementation, systemic corticosteroid and inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist
High-dose inhaled corticosteroid and inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist
Oxygen supplementation and high-dose inhaled corticosteroid alone
Inhaled long-acting beta-2 agonist plus oxygen supplementation
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 20; GINA 2024 Chapter 4
items.pearl: The ER trio for acute asthma is oxygen + repeated SABA + SYSTEMIC corticosteroid. Inhaled steroid does not replace systemic steroid in an exacerbation, and LABA alone has no role in rescue.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with acute severe asthma has been treated with nebulized salbutamol for 1 hour. He is now drowsy and unable to complete a sentence. PE: PR 130/min, RR 36/min, SpO2 95% on oxygen mask, markedly reduced breath sounds both lungs. ABG (on oxygen): pH 7.28, PaCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 22 mEq/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
choices: Prepare for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Reassure that the ABG is acceptable and continue nebulized salbutamol
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Start a beta-blocker to control the tachycardia
Discharge after one more nebulization because SpO2 is 95%
items.ref: GINA 2024 Chapter 4, life-threatening asthma
items.pearl: A NORMAL or RISING PaCO2 in acute asthma signals exhaustion: a tiring asthmatic should be hyperventilating (PaCO2 ~30). Drowsiness plus a silent chest means intubate, not observe.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with asthma uses inhaled salbutamol 4-5 times per week and wakes up breathless twice a month. She has never used a controller. Spirometry: FEV1 82% predicted with 14% and 220 mL improvement after bronchodilator. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment?
choices: Regular inhaled long-acting beta-2 agonist alone
items.ref: GINA 2024 Chapter 3, Step 2
items.pearl: GINA no longer accepts SABA-only treatment for any asthmatic. Every patient needs an ICS-containing regimen, and LABA is never given without ICS.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent sudden attacks of dyspnea with noisy breathing during stress. Attacks resolve within minutes and she is asymptomatic in between. During an attack, INSPIRATORY stridor is heard loudest over the neck; SpO2 is 98% and she does not respond to salbutamol. Spirometry between attacks is normal. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: GINA 2024, differential diagnosis of asthma
items.pearl: Inspiratory stridor loudest at the neck, normal SpO2, no response to bronchodilator and normal spirometry between attacks = extrathoracic upper airway obstruction, not asthma.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history has had exertional dyspnea and chronic cough for 3 months. PE: T 37.0 C, PR 80/min, RR 22/min, BP 140/80 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 97%, increased AP diameter of the chest wall, normal breath sounds. CXR shows increased lung volumes and flattened diaphragms. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate investigation to CONFIRM the diagnosis?
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 19; GOLD 2024
items.pearl: COPD cannot be diagnosed from CXR or symptoms. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is mandatory; PEFR is for monitoring asthma, not for diagnosing COPD.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man with COPD is able to perform daily activities but becomes breathless walking more than one block. PE: T 37.3 C, PR 90/min, RR 20/min, BP 140/80 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 96%, hyperinflation, hyperresonance to percussion and bilateral expiratory wheeze. He is already on appropriate inhaled therapy for his stage. Which of the following is indicated in the management of this condition?
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 18; GOLD 2024 Chapter 3
items.pearl: Pulmonary rehabilitation is indicated for any symptomatic COPD patient (mMRC 2 or more) already on optimal inhalers. Home oxygen needs proven resting hypoxemia; SpO2 96% does not qualify.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD is clinically stable on maximal inhaled therapy. Repeated ABG on room air 3 weeks apart shows PaO2 52 mmHg, PaCO2 46 mmHg and SpO2 86%. Hematocrit is 56%. Which of the following interventions will MOST improve his survival?
choices: Long-term oxygen therapy at least 15 hours per day
items.ref: GOLD 2024, long-term oxygen therapy; NOTT and MRC trials
items.pearl: Only smoking cessation, long-term oxygen (for PaO2 55 mmHg or less, or 59 mmHg or less with cor pulmonale/polycythemia), and lung volume reduction in selected patients improve survival in COPD.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD presents with 2 days of increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume and purulent sputum. PE: T 37.8 C, PR 110/min, RR 28/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, SpO2 88% on room air, diffuse expiratory wheeze, using accessory muscles, alert and oriented. ABG on room air: pH 7.25, PaCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 30 mEq/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management in addition to bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid, antibiotics and controlled oxygen?
items.ref: GOLD 2024 Chapter 5; ERS/ATS 2017 NIV guideline
items.pearl: In AECOPD with pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 45 mmHg in an alert, cooperative patient, NIV is first line and reduces mortality and intubation rate.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with well-controlled diabetes presents with fever and productive cough for 2 days. PE: T 38.5 C, PR 100/min, RR 22/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, SpO2 94% on room air; he is alert and fully oriented. Lab: BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management?
choices: Oral antibiotic as an outpatient with follow-up in 48-72 hours
Admission to an intensive care unit for intravenous antibiotic
Admission to a general ward for at least 7 days of intravenous antibiotic
Observation without antibiotics because the illness is likely viral
Immediate CT chest before starting any antibiotic
items.ref: IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP guideline; CURB-65 score
items.pearl: CURB-65 counts Confusion, Urea above 19 mg/dL (BUN above 19), RR 30 or more, BP below 90/60, age 65 or more. This patient scores 1 (age), so outpatient treatment is appropriate; stable comorbidity alone does not mandate admission.

items.stem: A 48-year-old alcoholic man has had fever, cough with foul-smelling sputum and weight loss for 3 weeks. He has poor dental hygiene. CXR shows a 5 cm cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial treatment?
choices: Intravenous clindamycin or ampicillin-sulbactam with postural drainage
Percutaneous catheter drainage as first-line therapy
Oral amoxicillin for 7 days as an outpatient
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Lung Abscess; IDSA aspiration pneumonia guidance
items.pearl: Aspiration lung abscess in an alcoholic with bad dentition is polymicrobial anaerobic. Antibiotics with anaerobic coverage for several weeks plus drainage; surgery is reserved for failure or massive hemoptysis.

items.stem: A 56-year-old diabetic man presents with fever, productive cough, nausea and vomiting for 3 days. PE: T 38.5 C, PR 110/min, RR 28/min, BP 95/55 mmHg, moderate dehydration, crepitation at the lower lung. Lab: glucose 128 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, Na 140 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, Cl 78 mEq/L, HCO3 12 mEq/L, albumin 4.0 g/dL. ABG: pH 7.40, PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 20 mmHg. Which of the following BEST explains his acid-base abnormality?
choices: Respiratory alkalosis from pneumonia, metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and high anion gap metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis alone
Respiratory alkalosis from pneumonia with high anion gap metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis from pneumonia with metabolic compensation
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from diarrhea and dehydration
items.ref: MED34/35 FA MCQ loop A+B item 15 with official explanation
items.pearl: Anion gap = 140 - 78 - 12 = 50 (delta AG 38) while delta HCO3 is only 12, so the ratio above 2 unmasks a coexisting metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Winter formula predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26 plus or minus 2; the measured 20 mmHg proves an added respiratory alkalosis. A NORMAL pH can hide three disorders.
items.source_note: ดัดแปลงตัวเลขจากต้นฉบับ MED34/35 FA MCQ ข้อ 15 (ต้นฉบับให้ pH 7.29 คู่กับ PaCO2 20 / HCO3 15 ซึ่งขัดกับ Henderson-Hasselbalch: ค่าชุดนั้นให้ pH 7.50) ปรับเป็น HCO3 12 / pH 7.40 เพื่อให้ตัวเลขสอดคล้องกัน โดยยังคงคำตอบและแนวคิด triple acid-base disorder เดิมไว้

items.stem: A 45-year-old man returns from a hotel stay with 5 days of fever, dry cough, diarrhea and confusion. PE: T 39.0 C, PR 90/min (relative bradycardia), RR 26/min, BP 110/70 mmHg. Lab: Na 126 mEq/L, ALT 120 U/L. CXR shows patchy consolidation of the left lower lobe. Which of the following is the MOST likely causative organism?
items.ref: IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP guideline; Harrison 21st ed., Legionella infections
items.pearl: Hyponatremia, transaminitis, diarrhea, confusion and relative bradycardia in a hotel or air-conditioning exposure is the classic Legionella picture; a urine antigen test gives the fastest answer.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has had cough for 4 weeks with low-grade fever, night sweats and 5 kg weight loss. CXR shows a right upper lobe infiltrate with cavitation. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial investigation?
choices: Sputum Xpert MTB/RIF with acid-fast bacilli smear
items.ref: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 3 (2021); Thai National TB Guideline 2021
items.pearl: A rapid molecular test on sputum is the first-line diagnostic for suspected active pulmonary TB. TST and IGRA detect infection, not disease, and cannot distinguish latent from active TB.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is newly diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. He is HIV-negative, has no previous TB treatment and normal liver and renal function. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate regimen?
choices: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin
6 months of isoniazid and rifampicin only
2 months of isoniazid and rifampicin followed by 7 months of isoniazid
2 months of four drugs followed by 10 months of isoniazid and ethambutol
items.ref: WHO TB treatment guideline 2022; Thai National TB Guideline 2021
items.pearl: Standard drug-susceptible regimen is 2IRZE / 4IR. Monotherapy at any stage breeds resistance; the continuation phase is extended only in special situations such as TB meningitis or bone TB.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man on 2IRZE for pulmonary TB returns at week 6 complaining that colours look washed out and his vision has blurred. Visual acuity is reduced bilaterally with impaired red-green discrimination. Liver enzymes are normal. Which drug is MOST likely responsible?
items.ref: WHO TB treatment guideline 2022, adverse drug reactions
items.pearl: Ethambutol causes dose-related retrobulbar optic neuritis with loss of red-green vision; isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine); rifampicin causes orange secretions; pyrazinamide raises uric acid.

items.stem: A patient with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted to a general medical ward. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate infection control precaution?
choices: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room with an N95 respirator for staff
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask for staff
Contact precautions with gown and gloves only
Standard precautions because transmission requires prolonged household contact
Protective isolation in a positive-pressure room
items.ref: WHO TB infection prevention and control 2019; CDC isolation precautions
items.pearl: TB spreads by droplet nuclei that stay airborne, so it needs a negative-pressure room and an N95. A positive-pressure room protects an immunocompromised patient and would push TB aerosols OUT into the ward.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with a pleural effusion undergoes thoracentesis. Pleural fluid protein 4.0 g/dL, pleural LDH 350 U/L; serum protein 6.5 g/dL, serum LDH 400 U/L (upper limit of normal 250 U/L). Which of the following is the correct interpretation?
choices: Exudate, because the fluid-to-serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5
Transudate, because the fluid-to-serum LDH ratio is below 0.6
Transudate, because pleural LDH is below the serum value
Exudate, but only if the fluid glucose is also below 60 mg/dL
Indeterminate without a pleural fluid cholesterol level
items.ref: Light RW, Light criteria; Harrison 21st ed., Disorders of the Pleura
items.pearl: One positive criterion is enough for exudate: protein ratio above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Here 4.0/6.5 = 0.62.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has had fever, pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea for 3 weeks. CXR shows a moderate right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid: exudate, 2,200 cells/mm3 with 85% lymphocytes, glucose 70 mg/dL, adenosine deaminase 78 U/L, AFB smear negative, cytology pending. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?
items.ref: MED OSCE/MEQ recall pleural fluid ADA 70; Harrison 21st ed., Tuberculous pleurisy
items.pearl: Lymphocyte-predominant exudate with ADA above 40 U/L in a young patient in an endemic country is tuberculous pleuritis; a negative AFB smear is expected because the fluid is paucibacillary.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with right lower lobe pneumonia remains febrile on day 3 of antibiotics. CXR shows a new moderate right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: turbid fluid, pH 7.10, glucose 35 mg/dL, LDH 1,800 U/L, Gram stain negative. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management?
choices: Insert an intercostal chest drain and continue antibiotics
Continue antibiotics alone and repeat the CXR in 1 week
Give intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy without drainage
Change to oral antibiotics and discharge
items.ref: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023; MEQ recall CAP with parapneumonic effusion
items.pearl: Pleural fluid pH below 7.20, glucose below 40 mg/dL, or a positive Gram stain or culture defines a COMPLICATED parapneumonic effusion: it will not resolve on antibiotics alone and needs tube drainage.

items.stem: A 22-year-old tall thin man has sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnea. PE: PR 88/min, RR 20/min, BP 120/70 mmHg, SpO2 (room air) 97%, slightly decreased breath sounds on the right, trachea midline. CXR shows a 10% right pneumothorax without mediastinal shift. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management?
choices: Observation with supplemental oxygen and a repeat chest radiograph
Needle decompression at the second intercostal space
items.ref: MED exam recall, pneumothorax 10% observe; BTS pleural disease guideline 2023
items.pearl: A small (under 2 cm), minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax is observed; high-flow oxygen speeds reabsorption about fourfold. Intervention is for large or symptomatic pneumothorax.

items.stem: While a central venous catheter is being inserted into the right subclavian vein, the patient becomes acutely dyspneic. PE: PR 140/min, RR 36/min, BP 70/40 mmHg, SpO2 82%, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the right with hyperresonance, trachea deviated to the left. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
choices: Immediate needle decompression of the right chest followed by chest drain insertion
Obtain an urgent portable chest radiograph before any intervention
Rapid intravenous fluid bolus and vasopressor infusion
Immediate endotracheal intubation with positive pressure ventilation
Urgent bedside echocardiography to exclude cardiac tamponade
items.ref: MED exam recall, tension pneumothorax during central line; ATLS 10th ed.
items.pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis: never wait for a film. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression makes the tension worse.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a childhood history of severe pneumonia has had a daily cough productive of large volumes of purulent sputum for years, with occasional hemoptysis. HRCT shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi with a signet-ring sign in the lower lobes. Which organism MOST commonly colonises the airway in this condition in a non-cystic-fibrosis host?
items.ref: MED exam recall, bronchiectasis pathogen; ERS bronchiectasis guideline 2017
items.pearl: Non-typeable H. influenzae is the commonest coloniser in non-CF bronchiectasis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa comes later with advanced disease and marks a worse prognosis.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with bronchiectasis has 3 exacerbations per year despite inhaled bronchodilators. He produces 60 mL of purulent sputum daily and sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate long-term management?
choices: Daily airway clearance physiotherapy with treatment of exacerbations and consideration of inhaled antibiotic
Routine cough suppressant to reduce sputum production
Surgical lobectomy for all patients with Pseudomonas colonisation
items.ref: ERS bronchiectasis guideline 2017; BTS bronchiectasis guideline 2019
items.pearl: Airway clearance is the backbone of bronchiectasis care. Cough suppressants are contraindicated when sputum must be cleared, and surgery is limited to localised disease that fails medical therapy.

items.stem: A 62-year-old obese woman with kyphoscoliosis is admitted with drowsiness. PE: RR 10/min, shallow breathing, SpO2 89% on room air. ABG on room air: pH 7.37, PaCO2 55 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg, HCO3 31 mEq/L. Which of the following BEST describes her respiratory failure?
choices: Chronic hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure from alveolar hypoventilation
Acute hypoxemic (type 1) respiratory failure from shunt
Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure without compensation
Pure metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Respiratory Failure; ABG interpretation
items.pearl: A high PaCO2 with a near-normal pH and a raised HCO3 means renal compensation has had days to work: this is CHRONIC type 2 failure. Hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2 with a normal A-a gradient.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with acute dyspnea. ABG on room air: pH 7.52, PaCO2 28 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 22 mEq/L. Assuming barometric pressure 760 mmHg, water vapour pressure 47 mmHg and respiratory quotient 0.8, which of the following BEST describes her gas exchange?
choices: Widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, indicating a gas exchange abnormality such as pulmonary embolism
Normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, indicating pure hyperventilation
Normal oxygenation because the PaO2 is above 60 mmHg
Low alveolar-arterial gradient from a right-to-left shunt
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Disturbances of Respiratory Function; B6.1.2 gas exchange
items.pearl: PAO2 = 0.21 x 713 - 28/0.8 = 150 - 35 = 115 mmHg, so the A-a gradient is 115 - 62 = 53 mmHg, far above the expected age-adjusted value of about 10. Hyperventilation alone never widens the gradient.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with severe pancreatitis develops worsening dyspnea on day 3. PE: RR 34/min, SpO2 88% on a non-rebreather mask, bilateral crackles. CXR shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function and no volume overload. He is intubated; PaO2/FiO2 is 120 mmHg on PEEP 10 cmH2O. ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 16 mEq/L. Which of the following ventilator strategies is MOST appropriate?
choices: Low tidal volume ventilation at 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight with plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O
Tidal volume 12 mL/kg of predicted body weight to correct the acidosis
High tidal volume with zero PEEP to avoid barotrauma
Pressure support ventilation alone without PEEP
Routine high-dose corticosteroid with tidal volume 10 mL/kg
items.ref: Berlin definition of ARDS 2012; ARDSNet ARMA trial; ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2017 guideline
items.pearl: Moderate ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 100-200 with PEEP of at least 5, bilateral infiltrates, not explained by cardiac failure). Only lung-protective low tidal volume ventilation has proven mortality benefit.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD is given oxygen 10 L/min via a face mask for dyspnea. One hour later he is drowsy. ABG on that oxygen: pH 7.22, PaCO2 88 mmHg, PaO2 190 mmHg, HCO3 35 mEq/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
choices: Reduce oxygen to target SpO2 88-92% and start non-invasive ventilation
Increase oxygen to keep SpO2 at 100%
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH
items.ref: BTS emergency oxygen guideline 2017; GOLD 2024
items.pearl: Uncontrolled oxygen in chronic hypercapnia worsens CO2 retention, mainly through loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and the Haldane effect. Titrate to 88-92% and ventilate; never abruptly remove oxygen.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain on day 5 after total knee replacement. PE: PR 118/min, RR 28/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 90% on room air, a swollen tender right calf, clear lungs. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and CXR is normal. Renal function is normal. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate investigation?
choices: D-dimer measurement to exclude the diagnosis
Ventilation-perfusion scan as the first-line test
Echocardiography as the definitive diagnostic test
items.ref: ESC 2019 Guidelines on acute pulmonary embolism
items.pearl: With a HIGH clinical probability, go straight to CTPA. D-dimer is only useful to rule out PE in low or intermediate probability; a positive D-dimer here would change nothing.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man with confirmed acute pulmonary embolism on CTPA has BP 78/50 mmHg despite 1,000 mL of intravenous fluid, PR 130/min and SpO2 88% on oxygen. Echocardiography shows right ventricular dilatation and hypokinesia. He has no bleeding, no recent surgery and no stroke. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment?
choices: Oral warfarin alone with a target INR of 2-3
Observation with oxygen and intravenous fluids
items.ref: ESC 2019 Guidelines on acute pulmonary embolism, high-risk PE
items.pearl: PE with persistent hypotension is high-risk PE: reperfusion with systemic thrombolysis is indicated unless absolutely contraindicated. IVC filters are for when anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails.

items.stem: A 68-year-old smoker with lung adenocarcinoma has a large recurrent left pleural effusion causing severe dyspnea. Cytology is positive for malignant cells and the lung re-expands fully after therapeutic thoracentesis, but the effusion recurs within 1 week. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate definitive management?
choices: Chest drain insertion with chemical pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter
Repeated therapeutic thoracentesis every week indefinitely
Diuretic therapy to reduce fluid re-accumulation
Systemic corticosteroid to suppress pleural inflammation
items.ref: MED exam recall, lung cancer with pleural effusion; BTS pleural disease guideline 2023
items.pearl: A recurrent malignant effusion with a lung that fully re-expands is best controlled by pleurodesis or an indwelling catheter. Trapped lung (incomplete re-expansion) makes pleurodesis fail, so a catheter is used instead.

items.stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker has 2 weeks of facial and upper limb swelling, worse when bending forward, with distended neck and chest wall veins. CXR shows a right upper mediastinal mass. He is alert with no stridor and SpO2 96%. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
choices: Contrast-enhanced CT chest and a tissue diagnosis before starting treatment
Immediate mediastinal radiotherapy without tissue diagnosis
High-dose diuretics to relieve the swelling
Reassurance and outpatient follow-up in 3 months
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Oncologic Emergencies, superior vena cava syndrome
items.pearl: SVC obstruction without airway compromise or cerebral edema is urgent but not immediately life-threatening: get the tissue diagnosis first, because treatment differs entirely for small cell carcinoma, lymphoma and germ cell tumour.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history has an 18 mm spiculated nodule in the right upper lobe found incidentally on CXR. He is asymptomatic. A CXR from 4 years ago is available and shows no nodule. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
choices: Contrast CT chest and tissue diagnosis with consideration of PET-CT for staging
items.ref: Fleischner Society 2017 guidelines; NCCN lung cancer screening and nodule evaluation
items.pearl: Size above 8 mm, spiculation, upper lobe location, a heavy smoking history and a new nodule since a prior film all raise malignancy risk: this needs CT, PET-CT and tissue, not watchful waiting.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has sneezing, clear rhinorrhea and nasal congestion for most days of the year, worse with house dust. Nasal examination shows pale, boggy, swollen turbinates. An oral antihistamine has given only partial relief. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next treatment?
items.ref: ARIA 2019 guideline; NL Syllabus B6.4 rational drug use
items.pearl: Intranasal corticosteroid is the most effective single agent for persistent moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis. Prolonged topical decongestant causes rhinitis medicamentosa.

items.stem: A 52-year-old obese man (BMI 34 kg/m2) snores loudly with witnessed apneas, wakes unrefreshed and falls asleep in meetings. BP is 150/95 mmHg on two drugs. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air
items.ref: AASM clinical practice guideline 2017; NL Syllabus 2.1.38 snoring
items.pearl: Snoring with witnessed apnea, daytime sleepiness and resistant hypertension is classic OSA; polysomnography is the diagnostic standard, and CPAP is first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe disease.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has had a sore throat and fever for 6 hours and now drools, sits leaning forward with his neck extended and has soft inspiratory stridor. He is anxious and refuses to lie down. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
choices: Keep the child calm and arrange airway management in the operating room by an experienced team
Examine the throat immediately with a tongue depressor
Give nebulized salbutamol and observe in the emergency room
Obtain a lateral neck radiograph in the radiology department first
Insert an intravenous line and take blood cultures before anything else
items.ref: Harrison 21st ed., Acute epiglottitis; Thai Pediatric airway emergency guidance
items.pearl: Drooling, tripod posture and stridor equal acute epiglottitis: any agitation or throat instrumentation can cause complete obstruction. Secure the airway first in a controlled setting.

items.scenario: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with fever, productive cough with rusty sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain for 4 days. PE: T 38.8 C, PR 112/min, RR 28/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, SpO2 90% on room air, dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds at the right lower lung and bronchial breathing above it. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation with blunting of the costophrenic angle. Lab: WBC 18,500/mm3 (PMN 88%), BUN 22 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.

questions.q: State the two most likely diagnoses that explain the whole picture.
questions.a: Community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe, with a parapneumonic pleural effusion.

questions.q: Calculate the CURB-65 score and state where this patient should be treated.
questions.a: CURB-65 = 2 (BUN above 19 mg/dL = 1, RR 28 is below 30 so 0, BP not below 90/60 so 0, no confusion, age 58 so 0). A score of 2 means admission to hospital for intravenous antibiotics.

questions.q: List four investigations on the pleural fluid you would request and give the one threshold value that decides whether a chest drain is needed.
questions.a: Cell count and differential, protein and LDH with paired serum (Light criteria), glucose and pH, Gram stain plus culture, AFB and ADA if TB is possible, and cytology. Pleural fluid pH below 7.20 (or glucose below 40 mg/dL, or positive Gram stain/culture) defines a complicated effusion needing chest tube drainage.

questions.q: Give the empirical antibiotic regimen for an admitted non-ICU patient with community-acquired pneumonia in Thailand.
questions.a: Intravenous ceftriaxone (or ampicillin-sulbactam) plus a macrolide such as azithromycin, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) as monotherapy.

questions.q: On day 3 he remains febrile with persistent effusion. State two next steps.
questions.a: Repeat imaging (ultrasound or CT chest) to assess for loculation or empyema, and drain the pleural space with an intercostal chest drain; consider intrapleural fibrinolytics or surgical referral if loculated, and review antibiotic coverage/cultures.

items.ref: MEQ recall: community-acquired pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion at right lower lung; IDSA/ATS 2019; BTS pleural disease guideline 2023
items.pearl: Fever persisting past 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics in pneumonia means look for a complication: empyema, lung abscess, or the wrong organism.

items.scenario: A 34-year-old man presents with cough for 6 weeks, blood-streaked sputum, low-grade fever, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. He lives with his wife and a 2-year-old child. PE: T 37.8 C, RR 22/min, SpO2 96%, crepitation at the right upper lung. CXR shows a right upper lobe infiltrate with a thin-walled cavity. HIV status is unknown.

questions.q: State the most likely diagnosis and the single most appropriate initial diagnostic test.
questions.a: Active pulmonary tuberculosis; sputum Xpert MTB/RIF together with AFB smear (with mycobacterial culture sent).

questions.q: Write the standard treatment regimen for a new drug-susceptible case, with the duration of each phase.
questions.a: Intensive phase 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (2IRZE), then continuation phase 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (4IR).

questions.q: Name two other tests you must perform at diagnosis and say why.
questions.a: HIV testing (co-infection changes prognosis and management) and baseline liver function tests with renal function and uric acid (INH/RIF/PZA hepatotoxicity, ethambutol dose adjustment in renal impairment). Visual acuity and colour vision testing before ethambutol is also expected.

questions.q: What isolation precaution is required while he is smear-positive, and what advice is given to the household?
questions.a: Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room where available, N95 respirator for staff, patient wears a surgical mask. Household contacts, especially the 2-year-old child, must be screened for TB disease and evaluated for latent TB infection and preventive therapy.

questions.q: Two weeks later he coughs up 400 mL of blood in 4 hours. State two immediate steps.
questions.a: Protect the airway: give oxygen, position the patient with the bleeding (right) side down, keep nil by mouth and prepare for intubation with a large-bore tube; resuscitate with fluids/blood and arrange urgent bronchial artery embolization (bronchoscopy if localisation is needed).

items.ref: WHO TB guidelines 2021-2022; Thai National TB Guideline 2021; MED OSCE recall chronic cough with AFB
items.pearl: Massive hemoptysis in old or active TB usually comes from a Rasmussen aneurysm or bronchial artery: bronchial artery embolization, not surgery, is the first definitive treatment.

items.scenario: A 72-year-old man with known COPD (FEV1 38% predicted) is brought in with 3 days of worsening dyspnea and increased purulent sputum. PE: T 37.6 C, PR 118/min, RR 30/min, BP 140/85 mmHg, SpO2 85% on room air, using accessory muscles, diffuse expiratory wheeze, no leg edema; he is alert and able to follow commands. ABG on room air: pH 7.25, PaCO2 70 mmHg, PaO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 30 mEq/L.

questions.q: Interpret the arterial blood gas completely.
questions.a: Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia: pH 7.25 is acidemic, PaCO2 70 mmHg is the primary disturbance, HCO3 30 mEq/L shows partial metabolic (renal) compensation indicating a chronic component; PaO2 48 mmHg on room air is severe hypoxemia. Type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure.

questions.q: State the oxygen target and how you would deliver it.
questions.a: Controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88-92% using a venturi mask (24-28%) or low-flow nasal cannula, avoiding high FiO2 which worsens hypercapnia.

questions.q: Name the ventilatory support indicated and two contraindications to it.
questions.a: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP), indicated for pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg. Contraindications include impaired consciousness or inability to protect the airway, cardiorespiratory arrest, facial trauma or surgery, copious secretions or vomiting, and hemodynamic instability.

questions.q: List the four pharmacologic components of treatment for this exacerbation.
questions.a: Inhaled short-acting bronchodilators (SABA with short-acting antimuscarinic), systemic corticosteroid (e.g. prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days), antibiotics (purulent sputum plus increased dyspnea and volume), and treatment of any precipitating cause.

questions.q: One hour after starting non-invasive ventilation the pH is 7.20 and he is now drowsy. What do you do?
questions.a: NIV has failed: proceed to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation, with ventilator settings that allow a prolonged expiratory time to avoid dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP).

items.ref: GOLD 2024 Chapter 5; BTS emergency oxygen guideline 2017; ERS/ATS 2017 NIV guideline
items.pearl: HCO3 30 mEq/L with PaCO2 70 mmHg tells you the kidney has been compensating for days; expect roughly 3-4 mEq/L HCO3 rise per 10 mmHg chronic PaCO2 rise, versus only 1 mEq/L in an acute rise.
